patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait unsteadiness and bilateral stiffness over the past year
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Darnell Henderson is a 75-year-old right-handed retired professor who presents to the neurology outpatient clinic accompanied by his wife, Helen, for evaluation of progressive gait difficulty and generalized stiffness that has been worsening over the past twelve to fourteen months. His wife first noticed changes approximately a year ago when he began walking more slowly and appeared less steady on his feet, particularly when navigating around furniture or stepping off curbs. Over the ensuing months, he has developed bilateral stiffness that he describes as feeling like his arms and legs are heavy and resistant to movement, worse in the mornings and improving somewhat with activity. He has not noticed a clear resting tremor, though his wife reports that she has occasionally seen his left hand trembling slightly when he is sitting and watching television, which he attributes to fatigue. He has noticed that his handwriting has become smaller and more cramped over the past six months, and he has had increasing difficulty buttoning his shirt in the mornings. His voice has become quieter according to family members, though he himself is not aware of this change. He has had two near-falls in the past three months, both occurring when he attempted to turn quickly while walking, but he has not actually fallen. His wife reports that he has become somewhat slower in his movements overall, taking longer to get dressed, to eat meals, and to complete household tasks. She has also noted that his facial expression seems less animated than it used to be, and friends have commented that he looks tired or unwell even when he feels fine. He continues to drive short distances in their neighborhood but has voluntarily stopped driving on the highway due to feeling less confident. He denies any urinary incontinence, significant cognitive decline, visual hallucinations, or acting out of dreams. His appetite has been reduced, which his gastroenterologist attributes to his gastroparesis, and he has lost approximately eight pounds over the past year. He has been taking metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for the past three years for gastroparesis. He reports that his symptoms have progressed gradually over the past year despite being on a stable dose of metoclopramide, and his wife believes the gait changes preceded the medication initiation, though she is not entirely certain of the timeline.

results.title: Drug-Induced Parkinsonism: A Review
results.key_finding: Drug-induced parkinsonism is the second most common cause of parkinsonism. Metoclopramide is among the most frequent causative agents. Key distinguishing features: DIP tends to be symmetric, develops within weeks to months of drug exposure, and resolves within weeks to months of drug discontinuation.

results.title: DaTscan in differentiating drug-induced parkinsonism from Parkinson's disease
results.key_finding: DaTscan (I-123 FP-CIT SPECT) shows normal dopamine transporter binding in drug-induced parkinsonism and reduced binding in Parkinson's disease, making it the most reliable imaging test to distinguish between the two conditions.

results.title: Metoclopramide-induced parkinsonism: clinical features and outcomes
results.key_finding: Chronic metoclopramide use can cause parkinsonism that may persist even after drug discontinuation, particularly in elderly patients. Some patients with metoclopramide-induced parkinsonism may have underlying subclinical PD that is unmasked by the dopamine-blocking drug.

output.summary: Metoclopramide is a well-established cause of drug-induced parkinsonism through central dopamine D2 receptor blockade. Differentiating DIP from idiopathic PD is critical and can be challenging, especially in elderly patients on chronic metoclopramide. Key differentiating features include: (1) DIP tends to be symmetric while PD is typically asymmetric; (2) DaTscan is normal in DIP but abnormal in PD; (3) DIP may resolve after drug discontinuation while PD is progressive; (4) metoclopramide may unmask underlying subclinical PD. A trial of metoclopramide discontinuation with clinical reassessment after 3-6 months is recommended, alongside DaTscan for definitive differentiation.

interactions: MAJOR: Metoclopramide is a dopamine receptor antagonist and directly opposes the mechanism of levodopa. Concurrent use significantly reduces levodopa efficacy and should be avoided.
MINOR: Metformin may slightly reduce levodopa absorption; administer at different times.
contraindications: Concurrent use with metoclopramide is a relative contraindication due to pharmacological antagonism at dopamine receptors.
warnings: Monitor for orthostatic hypotension when combining levodopa with lisinopril and tamsulosin
May cause nausea; take with food initially
alternatives: If metoclopramide cannot be discontinued, consider domperidone (not available in US) as a prokinetic alternative that does not cross the blood-brain barrier
Consider trimethobenzamide or ondansetron for gastroparesis symptom management as alternatives to metoclopramide

critical_actions: Apply MDS 2015 clinical diagnostic criteria for Parkinson's disease (bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity, supportive features, no absolute exclusion criteria)
Document temporal sequence of motor and non-motor (REM sleep behavior disorder, hyposmia, constipation, orthostatic intolerance) features
Review the full medication list for dopamine receptor antagonists (metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, antipsychotics) and any other agents that can mimic or worsen parkinsonism
Identify metoclopramide as a dopamine D2 receptor antagonist and discontinue it; substitute ondansetron, prucalopride, erythromycin, or (where available) domperidone
Recognize that premotor features (RBD, constipation, hyposmia) preceding metoclopramide use point to underlying idiopathic PD rather than pure DIP
Use DaTscan to differentiate underlying neurodegenerative PD (abnormal scan) from pure DIP (normal scan)
Do not start levodopa while the patient remains on metoclopramide because of pharmacological antagonism
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, or promethazine for nausea in a patient with parkinsonism

Do not prescribe typical antipsychotics (haloperidol, fluphenazine) or most atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine, aripiprazole) — restrict pharmacotherapy of psychosis to quetiapine, clozapine, or pimavanserin
Do not prescribe centrally acting anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl, benztropine) in older adults or in any patient with cognitive impairment
Do not continue metoclopramide in a patient with parkinsonism
Do not start levodopa while metoclopramide remains in the regimen
key_reasoning_points: Symmetric onset in a patient on metoclopramide creates diagnostic overlap between idiopathic PD and pure drug-induced parkinsonism
Premotor non-motor features that predate metoclopramide initiation point to underlying synucleinopathy
DaTscan is the critical differentiator: abnormal scan supports underlying neurodegenerative PD
RBD on polysomnography is a strong synucleinopathy biomarker and not caused by metoclopramide
Mother / family history of essential tremor (if present) is a red herring — ET and PD are distinct diseases
Metoclopramide has an FDA black-box warning against use beyond 12 weeks because of tardive dyskinesia risk

ET and PD are distinct conditions; PD diagnosis is established by motor and supportive criteria irrespective of family ET
